# Weekly Multi-Asset Market Briefing: AI Beta Roars Back As Software And Semis Lead

The past week delivered an aggressive momentum reversal across growth and AI-linked equities, with a pronounced snapback in software infrastructure, application software, and higher-beta semiconductors following a difficult prior month for many of these cohorts.[1] Against that backdrop, the watchlist skewed decisively positive, led by powerful upside in quantum computing, fintech, health-tech, and next-generation semiconductor names, while traditional energy and select cyclicals lagged. The move was broad rather than narrowly concentrated, with hyperscalers, high-quality compounders, and earlier-stage innovation assets all participating, setting the stage for an important debate: is this simply a positioning and short-covering rally, or the opening phase of a more durable re-acceleration in risk appetite into the second half of the year?[1]

## Market Overview

The dominant feature of the week was the re-emergence of AI and software beta as the key performance driver across the growth complex. The NASDAQ Composite advanced approximately 6.8% on the week and 10.5% on the month, signaling that the recent consolidation in high-multiple growth is giving way to renewed leadership from technology and adjacent sectors.[1] Within the watchlist, megacap hyperscalers participated meaningfully: Microsoft rose 14.0% on the week and 7.9% over the past month, while Meta gained 9.3% over the week and 11.8% over the month, and Alphabet’s class shares climbed 7.5% week-on-week and 10.8% on the month.[1] Amazon joined the move as well, adding 5.1% on the week and 19.4% on the month, underscoring that the rally was not confined to a narrow pocket of speculative names but extended to foundational AI and cloud platforms.[1]

The breadth and structure of the move are as notable as the magnitude. Several subsector baskets within the watchlist show synchronized double-digit weekly advances, especially in software infrastructure, application software, cybersecurity, semiconductors, and fintech.[1] The Software Infrastructure cluster saw Amplitude up 24.4%, Cloudflare up 20.4%, Datadog up 20.2%, Snowflake up 18.9%, Samsara up 18.4%, Procore up 17.5%, MongoDB up 16.6%, and Nutanix up 16.4% over the week.[1] Application Software mirrored that strength, with Hims & Hers Health up 48.3%, Oracle up 26.8%, RingCentral up 20.6%, Twilio up 19.1%, Guidewire up 19.0%, Atlassian up 17.1%, ServiceNow up 16.5%, and ServiceTitan up 16.3%.[1] This breadth inside software confirms an underlying factor move rather than isolated idiosyncratic events.

At the same time, the performance skew retains a clear factor tilt: the biggest winners generally have high operational leverage to AI, cloud, or digital transaction growth, and many were coming off materially depressed one-month bases. Names like Snowflake, Nutanix, Atlassian, ServiceNow, and FICO all posted weekly gains between roughly 10% and 20% while still showing negative one-month returns, highlighting how quickly sentiment has pivoted from capitulation to opportunistic re-risking.[1] The pattern is consistent with the classic playbook of a positioning-driven inflection where investors cover shorts and add selectively to secular winners following an earnings or macro scare.

The laggards on the week reinforce the view that this was a growth-led rotation rather than a broad risk-on across all factor exposures. Within Energy and Materials, several watchlist names declined meaningfully: CNH fell 8.5%, Devon lost 7.5%, Occidental dropped 7.2%, CF Industries declined 7.1%, Valero fell 6.3%, and California Resources declined 5.7% on the week.[1] This divergence between growth and cyclicals suggests that the incremental marginal dollar remains more attracted to long-duration cash flow stories and disruptive tech rather than to more traditional reflation or commodity narratives.

From a style perspective, the combination of strong performance in both profitable, high-quality franchises and in more speculative or earlier-stage growth is notable. For example, high-quality compounders such as Accenture, Roper, and Paychex delivered weekly advances in the mid- to high-single-digit range, while more volatile innovation plays like IonQ, Hims & Hers, Credo, Astera Labs, and Tera-tied semiconductor names posted outsized, often multi-decade type weekly returns.[1] The co-movement of quality and high-beta growth typically indicates a macro environment perceived as incrementally more benign for growth valuations, even absent specific new macro data points.

## Sector Leadership & Rotation

The sector leadership pattern this week was dominated by software and semiconductors. Software Infrastructure and Application Software both generated strong positive contribution, with broad-based double-digit weekly returns across multiple segments of the stack. In Software Infrastructure, Amplitude rose 24.4% on the week, Cloudflare 20.4%, Datadog 20.2%, Snowflake 18.9%, Samsara 18.4%, Procore 17.5%, MongoDB 16.6%, and Nutanix 16.4%.[1] These moves reversed a portion of the prior month’s drawdowns in many of these names, as one-month performance remains negative for several, including Snowflake at minus 16.9%, Nutanix at minus 3.4%, and Datadog at minus 3.5%.[1] The combination of strong secular narratives with recently de-risked expectations created fertile ground for a sharp factor snapback.

Application Software saw even more dramatic leadership, especially in health-tech and enterprise platforms. Hims & Hers Health surged 48.3% on the week and 24.5% on the month, making it one of the best performers across the entire watchlist.[1] Oracle posted a 26.8% weekly gain and 14.5% over the month, while RingCentral rose 20.6% on the week and 9.0% on the month.[1] Twilio advanced 19.1% weekly and 10.7% over the month, Guidewire gained 19.0% for the week despite being down 11.9% on the month, Atlassian rose 17.1% weekly while still down 8.9% on the month, ServiceNow climbed 16.5% on the week while down 15.0% on the month, and ServiceTitan rose 16.3% weekly while down 6.4% on the month.[1] The fact that several of these high-quality names remain negative on a one-month view despite strong weekly gains suggests potential room for further mean reversion if macro conditions remain supportive.

Cybersecurity staged a coordinated rebound after a period of underperformance and multiple stock-specific drawdowns earlier in the quarter. Tenable rose 20.6% on the week after a 4.9% decline over the past month, Varonis gained 20.0% while essentially flat on the month, Rubrik added 19.5% while roughly flat on a one-month basis, SentinelOne climbed 17.4%, Okta gained 14.8%, Zscaler rose 14.1%, Rapid7 added 12.0%, and CrowdStrike advanced 11.8% week over week while modestly down over the past month.[1] This pattern is consistent with a re-rating from oversold conditions and suggests incremental investor comfort that cybersecurity demand remains resilient even as some platform consolidation and pricing pressure narratives circulate.

Semiconductors were another key center of gravity for leadership, with an especially notable move in next-generation and AI-adjacent names rather than only the mega-cap GPU leader. IonQ, a quantum computing play, surged 60.1% on the week and 42.3% on the month, credibly ranking among the strongest moves anywhere in listed tech this period.[1] Credo gained 34.4% weekly and 58.0% on the month, SiTime advanced 19.8% on the week and 46.5% on the month, Cadence rose 17.1% and 7.4%, Astera Labs gained 16.8% and 37.8%, Synopsys climbed 14.6% and 4.9%, AMD rose 13.6% and 39.6%, and Onto Innovation advanced 13.1% and 44.0% over the same horizons.[1] Tower Semiconductor added 11.2% weekly and 59.5% on the month, highlighting the extent of enthusiasm for specialized analog and foundry exposures.[1]

The larger-cap semiconductor bellwethers also participated robustly. Intel rallied 9.8% on the week and an impressive 52.1% on the month, reflecting renewed optimism around its foundry strategy and domestic capacity build-out.[1] Broadcom gained 9.4% on the week and 28.7% on the month, Nvidia advanced 6.9% and 11.8%, and Marvell rose 8.7% on the week and 59.4% over the past month.[1] Micron gained 8.2% over the week while modestly negative at minus 1.4% for the month, while Seagate and Western Digital both rallied strongly, up 8.9% and 8.5% on the week and 34.7% and 22.2% on the month, respectively.[1] The alignment of memory, data storage, logic, and EDA all moving higher together underscores the broad-based nature of the AI and cloud-related capital expenditure cycle.

Fintech delivered another leg of outperformance, supported both by crypto-exposed and more traditional transaction-platform names. Affirm jumped 32.9% on the week and 45.2% on the month, Coinbase rose 22.9% weekly and 2.0% on the month, Block gained 14.6% and 23.2%, Shift4 climbed 12.4% and 12.9%, Bill Holdings advanced 11.8% while still down 2.9% for the month, Global Payments rose 10.6% and 3.9%, Synchrony added 8.2% and 20.2%, and Capital One gained 7.0% on the week and 14.6% on the month.[1] The combination of strong moves in both consumer credit and merchant acquirer names suggests that concerns about consumer health and transaction volumes have eased somewhat, or at least that the bar for negative surprises had moved higher after prior de-rating.

In contrast, traditional Energy and certain industrial cyclical exposures were relative underperformers. Within the Energy and Industrials subsector grouping, CNH Industrial fell 8.5% on the week despite a 4.6% gain on the month, Devon declined 7.5% both on the week and 8.2% on the month, Occidental lost 7.2% on the week and 7.9% on the month, CF Industries declined 7.1% weekly and 11.1% over the month, and Valero dropped 6.3% weekly and 6.2% monthly.[1] California Resources fell 5.7% on the week and 2.3% over the past month.[1] These moves show that while risk appetite improved, it skewed strongly toward long-duration growth and away from commodity and traditional reflation plays, which remain caught between demand concerns and policy uncertainty.

## Top Movers & Earnings Recap

The most dramatic moves on the watchlist were concentrated in a cluster of high-beta, innovation-driven names spanning quantum computing, health technology, semiconductors, software, and fintech. IonQ stands out as the single strongest performer, advancing 60.1% over the week and 42.3% over the month.[1] The magnitude of this move reflects a combination of factors: renewed interest in quantum computing as the next frontier of compute beyond classical and even GPU-dominated architectures, a relatively small float and high short-interest dynamic, and a broader investor willingness to take risk in earlier-stage technologies as AI enthusiasm spills over into adjacent compute paradigms. The market is increasingly viewing quantum as a potential long-term complement to AI workloads for specific classes of optimization and simulation problems, and IonQ has emerged as a liquid proxy for that thesis.

Hims & Hers Health, a telehealth and digital health platform, delivered another outsized move with a 48.3% weekly gain and 24.5% performance over the past month.[1] The stock’s strength sits at the intersection of several themes: the secular shift toward online care delivery and subscription health models, investor appetite for consumer-facing tech with visible revenue growth, and the narrative around potential profitability inflection as scale increases. The magnitude and persistence of the move over both weekly and monthly horizons suggest that investors are assigning higher credibility to the company’s ability to execute on its direct-to-consumer health vision while managing customer acquisition costs.

Credo Technology Group, a connectivity solutions provider leveraged to high-speed data, rose 34.4% over the week and 58.0% over the month, reflecting robust enthusiasm for suppliers that enable the higher-bandwidth networking demands of AI and accelerated computing clusters.[1] The move aligns with broader flows into the AI hardware supply chain beyond the obvious GPU winners, as investors seek secondary and tertiary beneficiaries of sustained data center capex. Similarly, Astera Labs gained 16.8% weekly and 37.8% on the month, and Onto Innovation rose 13.1% and 44.0% over the same intervals, further underscoring the strong bid for picks-and-shovels exposure to AI and advanced compute infrastructure.[1]

Fintech saw several notable top movers. Affirm gained 32.9% on the week and 45.2% on the month, while Coinbase rose 22.9% and 2.0%, and Block gained 14.6% weekly and 23.2% on the month.[1] The Affirm move is particularly significant because it follows a volatile period tied to credit quality concerns and cyclical fears; the recent price action indicates that investors are willing to re-engage with higher-risk consumer credit models when growth and engagement metrics surprise to the upside or when macro fears moderate. Coinbase’s performance, while strong on the week, is more modest on the month, suggesting some digestion of prior gains but renewed optimism in the platform’s role as a central venue for digital asset trading and potential beneficiary of institutionalization of crypto exposure.

Oracle’s 26.8% weekly gain and 14.5% monthly performance highlight the market’s enthusiasm for legacy enterprise software vendors that can pivot credibly into cloud and AI workloads.[1] The strength in Oracle fits into a broader pattern where investors are rewarding companies that demonstrate the ability to monetize AI through incremental cloud demand, database modernization, and generative AI–enabled services. In parallel, application software names like RingCentral, up 20.6% on the week, Twilio up 19.1%, and Atlassian up 17.1% show that the market is again assigning value to communications and collaboration platforms after a period of skepticism around post-pandemic growth normalization.[1]

Several observably oversold software and analytics names also executed powerful weekly reversals despite still-weak one-month trajectories. Snowflake rallied 18.9% on the week, yet remains down 16.9% on the month, highlighting how quickly sentiment can reverse when expectations are derisked.[1] Nutanix gained 16.4% weekly but is still down 3.4% on the month, FICO rose 16.4% weekly while down 10.8% on the month, and Elastic advanced 9.8% weekly while still down 14.7% over the month.[1] For long-term investors, these dynamics illustrate a market environment where strong franchises can experience sharp multiple compression on short-term execution risk or guide-downs, only to re-rate quickly when investors conclude that long-term demand remains intact.

On the negative side of the ledger, the week’s underperformers were heavily skewed toward traditional Energy and Materials. CNH Industrial declined 8.5% on the week while still up 4.6% on the month, indicating some consolidation after prior strength.[1] Devon Energy dropped 7.5% weekly and 8.2% on the month, Occidental fell 7.2% and 7.9%, CF Industries declined 7.1% and 11.1%, Valero dropped 6.3% and 6.2%, and California Resources fell 5.7% and 2.3% over the same intervals.[1] These moves may reflect a combination of demand-related concerns, volatility in underlying commodity benchmarks, and a relative rotation away from energy toward higher-growth digital and AI exposures as investors reassess risk-reward across sectors.

In the broader communication services and media complex, performance was more mixed. Comcast rose 6.1% on the week and 3.7% on the month, while Netflix actually declined 5.5% on the week despite being up 2.8% on the month.[1] Pinterest, more squarely positioned as a digital advertising platform with commerce adjacency, gained 14.2% on the week and 7.2% over the month, while The Trade Desk rose 11.8% on the week but remains down 4.6% over the month.[1] This dispersion within ad-driven business models underscores the importance of idiosyncratic factors such as product roadmaps, measurement capabilities, and sensitivity to macro advertising cycles.

Notably, there were no watchlist earnings events scheduled for the next two weeks, which means the week’s price action was more about macro positioning, factor flows, and thematic narratives than about discrete quarterly reports.[1] In that context, the breadth and magnitude of the rally in growth and AI-linked names may partly reflect the absence of near-term earnings catalysts that could create fresh idiosyncratic downside, effectively lowering the perceived event risk and emboldening investors to add exposure.

## Macro & Rates Environment

Even without introducing specific new macro datapoints or yield levels, the cross-asset rotation within the watchlist and broader indices offers useful clues about how investors are processing the macro backdrop. The renewed strength in long-duration, cash-flow–backed technology franchises, together with the sharp beta snapback in earlier-stage growth, suggests that markets are incrementally more comfortable with the path of policy and the growth-inflation mix than they were several weeks ago. The outperformance of the NASDAQ Composite, which gained 6.8% on the week and 10.5% on the month, points toward a constructive environment for growth-oriented valuations.[1]

At the same time, the persistent underperformance of traditional Energy and Materials within the watchlist speaks to ongoing uncertainty around the global demand outlook and the durability of commodity price strength. With Devon, Occidental, CF Industries, Valero, and California Resources all posting weekly declines of roughly 6% to 8%, and with several also showing negative one-month performance, the signal is that investors are not yet prepared to price in a robust, synchronized industrial upswing.[1] Instead, the market appears to be favoring secular growth narratives whose earnings trajectories are less directly tied to near-term cyclical conditions.

Financials provide a complementary lens into macro sentiment. On the one hand, consumer credit–sensitive names such as Synchrony and Capital One delivered solid weekly gains of 8.2% and 7.0%, respectively, and strong one-month performance of 20.2% and 14.6%.[1] This suggests that market participants are not overly concerned about an imminent deterioration in consumer balance sheets or credit performance. On the other hand, fintech and payments platforms with more explicit growth narratives, such as Affirm, Coinbase, Block, and Shift4, registered significantly larger gains, pointing to a preference for growth and innovation within the financials ecosystem rather than a broad-based, value-driven rotation into the sector.[1]

The rally in semiconductors and AI hardware proxies has macro implications as well. The strong one-month moves in Intel at 52.1%, Marvell at 59.4%, Tower Semiconductor at 59.5%, Credo at 58.0%, and Seagate at 34.7% imply that the market is increasingly confident in a multi-year capital expenditure cycle focused on AI infrastructure, domestic re-shoring of critical semiconductor capacity, and ongoing growth in data creation and storage.[1] This capital spending cycle serves as a partial counterweight to concerns about slower cyclical growth, particularly in manufacturing-oriented regions, by providing a structurally higher level of tech-related investment.

Within healthcare and life sciences, the picture is more nuanced but still constructive for risk-taking. UnitedHealth gained 6.7% on the week and 14.2% on the month, Thermo Fisher rose 6.2% and 13.3%, Novo Nordisk advanced 8.0% and 8.2%, and IQVIA gained 5.5% and 5.7% over the same horizons.[1] These moves indicate that investors continue to favor defensive growth and innovation in healthcare, particularly where supported by strong secular demand drivers such as aging populations, chronic disease management, and novel therapies. The fact that these names performed well alongside higher-beta tech and fintech suggests a broader risk-on posture rather than a narrow barbell between defensives and growth.

It is also noteworthy that the rally in growth and AI-linked names occurred without any imminent watchlist earnings catalysts, as there are no earnings scheduled for the next two weeks.[1] In the absence of near-term micro events, macro narratives and positioning can dominate price action. The recent pattern implies that many investors were underweight high-growth and AI exposures after prior volatility and have been forced to chase performance as prices inflected higher. From a forward-looking perspective, this positioning dynamic matters because it may amplify both upside and downside volatility around the next set of macro or policy surprises.

## Watchlist Deep Dives

### Hyperscalers and AI Platforms: MSFT, AMZN, GOOG, META

The hyperscalers remain central to any discussion of the AI and cloud investment cycle, and all four major watchlist names delivered strong weekly and monthly performance. Microsoft rose 14.0% on the week and 7.9% on the month, reinforcing its position as a core AI and enterprise software platform.[1] The stock’s outperformance relative to many peers reflects the market’s conviction in the breadth of Microsoft’s AI monetization pathways, spanning Azure infrastructure, AI-infused productivity and collaboration tools, and the integration of large language model capabilities into core Office and Dynamics suites. The solid one-month performance, though less explosive than some higher-beta names, underscores Microsoft’s status as a foundational compounder rather than a tactical trade.

Amazon gained 5.1% on the week and 19.4% on the month, benefiting from a combination of improving sentiment around consumer discretionary spending, continued strength in its advertising and third-party marketplace businesses, and renewed enthusiasm for AWS as a key beneficiary of AI workloads.[1] The company’s ability to leverage AI across retail, logistics, and cloud services creates multiple avenues for value creation, and the robust one-month move indicates that investors are increasingly willing to pay for those options. Amazon’s performance, though more measured than some smaller-cap AI names, aligns with the pattern of investors using megacaps as liquid vehicles to express structural AI and e-commerce views.

Alphabet’s class shares advanced 7.5% on the week and 10.8% on the month, while Meta rose 9.3% and 11.8% over the same periods.[1] For Alphabet, the key debate remains the balance between AI-driven innovation in Search and the potential for margin pressure from heavier AI inference costs and more capital-intensive infrastructure. The stock’s strong performance suggests that investors currently assign greater weight to the upside from AI-enhanced search experiences, YouTube monetization, and cloud growth than to concerns about expense intensity. Meta’s gains reflect progress in monetization efficiency, ongoing traction in Reels, and an emerging AI assistant and model narrative layered on top of its core social platforms.

Across these four names, the common thread is that the market is rewarding those platforms that can show practical, near- to medium-term AI monetization paths rather than purely aspirational roadmaps. Their strong performance also provides a stabilizing anchor for the broader growth complex; as long as hyperscalers trade well, investors are likely to remain engaged with second- and third-order AI beneficiaries.

### Flagship AI Hardware and Semis: NVDA, AVGO, AMD, INTC, MRVL, ARM, TSM

Nvidia remains the emblematic AI hardware leader, and while its weekly and monthly moves are less extreme than some smaller-cap names, they remain meaningfully positive. Nvidia gained 6.9% on the week and 11.8% on the month, reflecting continued confidence in its dominant position in accelerated computing and data center GPUs.[1] The stock’s performance, though relatively more modest on a percentage basis than certain high-beta peers, must be viewed in the context of its size and prior appreciation. Investors are now focused on the sustainability of demand beyond first-wave hyperscaler deployments, including enterprise AI, sovereign AI, and new verticals such as automotive and industrial automation.

Broadcom, another key player in the AI infrastructure stack, rose 9.4% on the week and 28.7% over the month.[1] The strength in Broadcom speaks to its diversified exposure across custom AI accelerators, networking, and software, providing a somewhat less volatile but still strongly levered play on the AI capex cycle. The nearly thirty percent one-month move emphasizes how aggressively investors are re-rating companies that can provide critical silicon and connectivity for AI data centers.

AMD gained 13.6% on the week and 39.6% on the month, underscoring its emergence as the principal challenger to Nvidia in AI accelerators and as a beneficiary of broader compute demand.[1] The stock’s outperformance relative to Nvidia over the past month likely reflects the asymmetry inherent in being the number two player in a rapidly expanding market, combined with optionality in client and server CPUs. Intel’s 9.8% weekly gain and 52.1% monthly performance are similarly notable, signaling growing investor belief that the company can participate in AI-related demand and execute on its foundry and process technology roadmaps.[1]

Marvell’s 8.7% weekly and 59.4% monthly gains highlight the market’s enthusiasm for high-speed networking and custom silicon providers, both of which are critical to scaling AI clusters.[1] Arm Holdings, up 11.9% on the week and 29.9% on the month, and Taiwan Semiconductor, while not specifically quantified in this week’s precomputed set, remain central to the broader ecosystem, supplying architectures and manufacturing capabilities essential to the AI era.[1] Together, these moves reinforce the notion that investors see the AI hardware and semiconductor cycle as multi-year in nature, with meaningful upside still to be realized across multiple layers of the value chain.

### Quantum and Next-Gen Compute: IONQ

IonQ’s 60.1% weekly and 42.3% monthly performance is emblematic of the speculative yet increasingly institutionally interesting corner of the compute landscape beyond classical architectures.[1] As a pure-play quantum computing company with a differentiated trapped-ion approach, IonQ serves as a proxy for investor sentiment toward the long-tail potential of quantum as a complement to AI. The stock’s explosive move can be partly attributed to technical and positioning factors, including high short interest and a relatively limited float, which can exacerbate moves when incremental demand increases.

However, the broader context matters as well. As AI becomes more established as a foundational technology, investors are naturally looking ahead to what may drive the next leg of computational breakthroughs. Quantum computing is frequently cited in that conversation, particularly for use cases such as complex optimization, cryptography, and molecular simulation. IonQ’s strong price action indicates that a subset of investors is willing to allocate capital to early-stage platforms that may not have near-term commercial scale but could occupy strategic importance over a multi-decade horizon. For portfolio construction, this suggests that maintaining a small sleeve for such speculative innovation plays can provide convex exposure to future compute paradigms, albeit with significant volatility.

### Software Infrastructure & Data: SNOW, DDOG, MDB, NTNX, IOT, AMPL, DT, ESTC

The software infrastructure and data analytics cohort delivered one of the strongest subsector rebounds this week, reversing a portion of the drawdowns experienced over the prior month. Snowflake rose 18.9% on the week but remains down 16.9% on the month, highlighting the depth of the prior correction and the violence of the subsequent snapback.[1] The market is re-engaging with Snowflake’s long-term data cloud thesis, even as near-term consumption trends and optimization efforts from customers create some volatility in reported metrics. For fundamental investors, the key question remains the balance between slowing headline growth rates and the durability of the platform’s competitive moat.

Datadog gained 20.2% on the week while still down 3.5% over the month, reflecting a similar dynamic of recovery from oversold conditions as investors reaffirm their belief in the centrality of observability platforms in complex, cloud-native environments.[1] MongoDB’s 16.6% weekly gain, against a 1.9% decline over the month, reinforces that de-rating in high-quality, high-growth database and developer platform names can provide opportunities when sentiment overshoots to the downside.[1] Nutanix, which rose 16.4% on the week and is down 3.4% over the month, straddles the line between legacy and modern infrastructure and is benefiting from renewed enthusiasm around hybrid cloud architectures.[1]

Samsara’s 18.4% weekly gain, despite a 9.1% decline over the month, highlights investor interest in applied AI platforms that can drive operational efficiency for physical operations through sensor data and analytics.[1] Amplitude’s 24.4% weekly move, with only a 1.0% decline over the month, indicates a somewhat cleaner base and potential early re-rating of analytics as a critical component of product-led growth strategies.[1] Dynatrace’s 10.0% weekly gain against an 11.5% monthly decline and Elastic’s 9.8% weekly gain against a 14.7% monthly decline likewise underscore the broader theme: where software infrastructure platforms remain integral to digital transformation and AI adoption, sharp de-ratings can prove transitory if fundamentals hold.

### Application Software Platforms: NOW, CRM, WDAY, TEAM, INTU, HUBS, ZM, TTAN

Enterprise application software names experienced a strong relief rally, though with notable dispersion when viewed over a one-month horizon. ServiceNow rose 16.5% on the week but remains down 15.0% on the month, Salesforce gained 10.4% weekly while down 6.3% on the month, Workday climbed 10.1% weekly but is down 6.4% monthly, and Atlassian rose 17.1% weekly while down 8.9% over the month.[1] These patterns reflect a market that had aggressively de-rated high-growth, high-multiple applications names on concerns about enterprise IT spending, elongating deal cycles, and AI-driven disruption, only to see a rapid partial reversal when those fears proved at least somewhat overstated.

Intuit gained 12.1% on the week but is down 12.0% on the month, HubSpot rose 15.7% on the week while down 15.1% on the month, and Zoom climbed 11.1% weekly and 15.2% monthly.[1] Intuit’s move reflects resilience in small business and consumer tax and financial software demand, while HubSpot’s performance suggests that marketing and CRM platforms with strong product-market fit can still command investor attention despite fears of budget compression. Zoom’s gains indicate that the market is increasingly viewing it not only as a pandemic-era beneficiary but as an ongoing platform for unified communications with AI-enhanced features.

ServiceTitan’s 16.3% weekly advance and 6.4% monthly decline highlight the continued investor appetite for vertical software platforms that digitize specific trades and service industries, offering attractive unit economics and high customer stickiness.[1] Across the group, the key medium-term question is the extent to which generative AI will act as a tailwind, enabling higher-value workflows and richer automation, versus a headwind, by compressing the value of certain software modules. The current price action suggests that the market is leaning toward the former interpretation, particularly for platforms that are already embedding AI into their roadmaps.

### Cybersecurity: CRWD, PANW, ZS, S, OKTA, TENB, VRNS, RPD, RBRK

Cybersecurity saw a synchronized rebound, with nearly all key names in the watchlist delivering double-digit weekly gains. CrowdStrike advanced 11.8% on the week, Palo Alto Networks 7.8%, Zscaler 14.1%, SentinelOne 17.4%, Okta 14.8%, Tenable 20.6%, Varonis 20.0%, Rapid7 12.0%, and Rubrik 19.5%.[1] The moves come after a period of heightened concern about platform consolidation, pricing pressure, and the potential for AI to alter the threat landscape and defense playbook. The rebound indicates that investors still view cybersecurity as a non-discretionary budget item, with AI likely to serve as both a source of incremental threats and a powerful tool for defenders.

The dispersion in one-month performance is instructive. While CrowdStrike is down 2.7% on the month and Palo Alto roughly flat at minus 0.6%, Zscaler is down 13.7%, Tenable down 4.9%, Rapid7 down 8.2%, and Varonis down 1.1%.[1] Okta is down 7.9% and SentinelOne 2.5% over the month.[1] These data points underscore that the weekly rallies are largely partial recoveries from prior drawdowns rather than new highs. For long-term investors, this dynamic can be attractive because it signals that valuations may still be reasonable relative to the secular growth trajectory, especially for platforms with expanding modules and strong net retention.

Rubrik’s 19.5% weekly gain and modest 0.5% one-month performance highlight emerging interest in data security, backup, and resilience as complementary layers to traditional endpoint and network security.[1] The integration of cyber and data protection is likely to be a key theme as enterprises re-architect for zero trust and AI-driven environments. Overall, the cybersecurity complex remains a core structural overweight in many growth portfolios, and this week’s action reinforces that investors are inclined to buy dips when macro and idiosyncratic fears become excessive.

### Fintech & Payments: AFRM, COIN, XYZ, FOUR, BILL, GPN, SYF, COF

Fintech and payments names on the watchlist delivered strong performance, with Affirm, Coinbase, Block, Shift4, Bill, Global Payments, Synchrony, and Capital One all registering meaningful weekly gains.[1] Affirm’s 32.9% weekly and 45.2% monthly performance points to a substantial re-rating as investors reassess the company’s ability to manage credit risk and drive transaction growth in a still-resilient consumer spending environment.[1] The move also likely reflects short covering, given the high sensitivity of buy-now-pay-later models to macro narratives and regulatory headlines.

Coinbase rose 22.9% on the week and 2.0% on the month, evidencing its continued role as a liquid proxy for broader digital asset sentiment.[1] While crypto markets remain volatile, the company’s platform position and regulatory engagement give it a unique standing among listed fintech names. Block gained 14.6% on the week and 23.2% on the month, benefiting from improving sentiment around its consumer and merchant ecosystems, including Cash App and Square, as well as optionality around Bitcoin-related initiatives.[1]

Shift4 Payments advanced 12.4% weekly and 12.9% monthly, Global Payments rose 10.6% and 3.9%, Bill gained 11.8% while still down 2.9% on the month, Synchrony added 8.2% and 20.2%, and Capital One climbed 7.0% and 14.6% over the same periods.[1] These moves underscore that investors are increasingly willing to re-engage with both cyclical consumer credit exposures and structural digital payments winners as fears of an abrupt deterioration in consumer health recede. However, the stronger moves in higher-beta names like Affirm and Coinbase relative to more diversified processors and banks highlight a continued preference for growth and optionality over pure value within financials.

### Consumer & E-Commerce: SHOP, GCT, GLBE, SE, FIVE, NKE, GDDY, HIMS

Consumer and e-commerce exposures within the watchlist were broadly positive, led by Shopify and GigaCloud among digital commerce names and Hims & Hers in health tech. Shopify rose 18.4% on the week and 6.0% on the month, underscoring renewed confidence in the company’s ability to drive merchant solutions revenue and leverage AI to optimize commerce experiences.[1] GigaCloud gained 16.3% on the week and 21.6% on the month, reflecting enthusiasm for asset-light, marketplace-oriented business models in cross-border commerce.[1] Global-e Online rose 12.2% on the week with a relatively flat minus 0.3% performance over the month, pointing to a more modest but still constructive re-rating as investors balance strong cross-border e-commerce growth with execution risk.[1]

Sea Limited gained 6.3% on the week and 8.1% over the month, suggesting that concerns about competitive intensity and policy risk in its core markets have eased somewhat.[1] GoDaddy advanced 8.1% and 1.9% over the same intervals, benefiting from its role in enabling the digital presence of small businesses and individuals.[1] Five Below’s 8.7% weekly and 11.2% monthly gains demonstrate that select specialty retailers can still perform well when they deliver compelling value propositions and store productivity, even amid broader consumer uncertainty.[1]

Nike’s 8.0% weekly gain, despite a 13.9% decline over the month, indicates some early signs of stabilization after a period of disappointment around growth and inventory dynamics.[1] Hims & Hers, with its 48.3% weekly and 24.5% monthly performance, stands out not only within health tech but across the entire consumer complex, highlighting the power of subscription models and direct-to-consumer engagement when combined with a differentiated brand and product offering.[1] For portfolio allocators, the message is that consumer-facing tech and platforms with strong unit economics and optionality around AI and personalization remain attractive despite macro noise.

### Data Storage & Infrastructure: STX, WDC, PSTG, DOCN, ANET, NET, FSLY

The data storage and cloud infrastructure ecosystem also participated in the rally, reflecting confidence in the durable demand for data creation, storage, and transmission. Seagate rose 8.9% on the week and 34.7% on the month, while Western Digital gained 8.5% and 22.2% over the same periods.[1] These moves align with the view that the memory and storage cycle is in an upswing, supported by AI and high-performance computing workloads. The magnitude of the one-month gains underscores how quickly investor sentiment has moved from cycle trough concerns to pricing in a stronger recovery.

In cloud infrastructure, DigitalOcean rose 13.3% on the week and 3.8% on the month, Arista Networks gained 11.5% and 20.7%, and Fastly rose 6.5% while down 8.6% on the month.[1] These names collectively illustrate different ways to play the ongoing transition to cloud and edge computing. Arista, in particular, is seen as a critical supplier of high-speed networking for AI clusters, while DigitalOcean provides accessible cloud infrastructure for developers and small businesses. Fastly, after prior volatility, remains a higher-risk, higher-reward edge platform tied to traffic and security trends.

Cloudflare’s 20.4% weekly gain, despite a 10.9% decline over the month, and the 9.9% weekly gain for the cloud storage–linked name labeled PSTG with a 4.0% monthly gain further reinforce the attractiveness of owning leveraged plays on internet traffic, security, and content delivery where fundamentals remain robust.[1] For investors, the core insight is that while these names can be sensitive to macro narratives around IT spending, their long-term drivers are tied to structural growth in data and compute rather than short-term cycles.

### Industrial and Vertical Software: TRMB, ROP, BSY, TYL, MANH, PCOR, GWRE

Industrial and vertical software platforms continued to gain traction as investors look for ways to express exposure to digital transformation in physical industries. Trimble rose 7.0% on the week and 5.7% on the month, Roper gained 5.6% and 3.3%, Bentley Systems advanced 12.1% on the week while down 5.5% on the month, Tyler Technologies rose 8.0% on the week with a modest 0.4% decline over the month, Manhattan Associates gained 9.8% weekly while down 4.0% over the month, Procore rose 17.5% on the week while down 5.6% monthly, and Guidewire gained 19.0% on the week while down 11.9% on the month.[1]

These platforms generally benefit from high switching costs, specialized workflows, and long runway for digitization in fields such as construction, public sector, insurance, and supply chain. The recent performance suggests that investors are willing to look through near-term cyclical noise in these end markets to the longer-term value of software-led efficiency gains. However, the negative one-month returns for several names indicate that the space is not immune to macro concerns; instead, it offers an attractive middle ground between secular growth and sensitivity to real-world capex and project cycles.

### Healthcare & Life Sciences: UNH, TMO, NVO, IQV, ABT, ZTS

Within healthcare and life sciences, the watchlist names showed solid, if less explosive, performance. UnitedHealth rose 6.7% on the week and 14.2% on the month, Thermo Fisher gained 6.2% and 13.3%, Novo Nordisk advanced 8.0% and 8.2%, and IQVIA gained 5.5% and 5.7%.[1] These moves underscore the role of healthcare as a defensive growth anchor in portfolios, particularly when macro uncertainty persists but risk appetite for tech and fintech is rising.

Abbott and Zoetis, while not explicitly quantified in the precomputed set for this week, continue to represent high-quality franchises with attractive exposure to diagnostics, devices, and animal health innovation.[1] The combination of these names with the more volatile tech complex allows investors to balance portfolio beta while maintaining exposure to innovation-driven secular growth. The key medium-term question for this space is how policy and reimbursement dynamics evolve, but in the current environment, the sector appears well-positioned as a core allocation.

## Upcoming Catalysts

Over the next two weeks, there are no watchlist companies scheduled to report earnings, which has important implications for how the market may trade.[1] In the absence of near-term micro catalysts, macro narratives, positioning dynamics, and thematic flows are likely to continue to dominate price action across the watchlist. For the high-beta software and semiconductor names that have already seen substantial short-covering and factor-driven rallies, this can cut both ways: on the upside, a lack of imminent earnings risk may embolden further accumulation; on the downside, absent new information, some investors may choose to take profits into strength.

The strong one-month moves in many AI and semiconductor names, such as Intel at 52.1%, Marvell at 59.4%, Tower Semiconductor at 59.5%, Credo at 58.0%, and Onto Innovation at 44.0%, create a high base from which the next macro or policy surprise will be interpreted.[1] If upcoming macro data or central bank communication is perceived as supportive of sustained growth with manageable inflation, the AI capex and secular growth narratives could continue to drive incremental flows into these names. Conversely, any material shift in the policy or growth outlook could trigger a reversal, particularly in the more speculative corners of the space.

For software, the key catalysts will be developments in AI product roadmaps, pricing strategies, and platform consolidation narratives. Names like ServiceNow, Salesforce, Workday, Atlassian, Snowflake, Datadog, and MongoDB have all seen sharp weekly rebounds off de-rated bases, but their one-month returns remain mixed.[1] Investors will be attuned to any signposts around enterprise AI adoption, consumption trends, and the ability of these platforms to monetize AI features without eroding their existing revenue models.

In fintech, the strong performance of Affirm, Coinbase, Block, and Shift4 sets up a period where regulatory and macro news flow could have outsized impact on sentiment.[1] Any major developments in digital asset regulation, payments innovation, or consumer credit conditions could act as catalysts for further re-rating or correction. The same holds for consumer and e-commerce names like Shopify, Sea, GigaCloud, and Hims & Hers, where investor focus will be on user growth, engagement, and monetization trends in the absence of near-term earnings prints.[1]

## What To Watch Next Week

Looking ahead, the central question for next week is whether the powerful factor rotation into growth, AI, and software can sustain without immediate earnings validation. The breadth and magnitude of the rally, with the NASDAQ up 6.8% on the week and a wide range of watchlist names posting double-digit weekly gains, raises the possibility of some consolidation or mean reversion.[1] Yet the underlying drivers—structural AI capex, digital transformation, and resilient consumer and enterprise demand for key platforms—remain intact, providing a fundamental backbone for the moves.

For semiconductors and AI hardware, investors should monitor whether the recent leaders like Intel, AMD, Marvell, Broadcom, and the more specialized names such as Credo, Astera Labs, SiTime, and Onto Innovation can hold their gains.[1] Sustained strength would signal that the market is willing to continue re-rating the entire AI hardware value chain higher, while any abrupt pullback might indicate that near-term positioning has become extended. Similarly, IonQ’s ability to consolidate after a 60.1% weekly move will provide a barometer of speculative appetite in the quantum and next-gen compute space.[1]

In software, attention will focus on whether the rebound in infrastructure, data, application, and cybersecurity names evolves into a more durable trend or proves to be a short-lived short-covering rally. The mixed one-month performance profiles of Snowflake, Nutanix, FICO, Elastic, ServiceNow, Salesforce, Workday, Atlassian, and others create both risk and opportunity.[1] Sustained follow-through would indicate that investors are willing to rebuild longer-term positions in these platforms, while a drift lower in the absence of news could suggest that some participants are still using strength to reduce exposure.

Fintech and consumer tech will also remain in focus. After outsized weekly gains for Affirm, Coinbase, Block, Shopify, GigaCloud, and Hims & Hers, the next week will test whether incremental buyers are still willing to step in at higher levels.[1] The behavior of more defensive but still growth-oriented names like UnitedHealth, Thermo Fisher, Novo Nordisk, and IQVIA, which posted mid-single to high-single-digit weekly gains, will help gauge whether investors maintain a balanced risk posture or pivot back toward defensives.[1]

For portfolio construction, this is an environment that favors selective risk-taking. The watchlist data show a clear reassertion of growth and AI leadership, but also emphasize that many high-quality names are only partially recovered from prior drawdowns. In that sense, the opportunity set remains rich, but volatility is likely to stay elevated. Allocators should focus on balancing exposure between proven compounders in hyperscale, semiconductors, and healthcare, and carefully sized positions in higher-beta software, fintech, and innovation plays where the payoff profile is asymmetric but path-dependent.

In sum, the week marked a powerful reaffirmation of the centrality of AI, software, and digital platforms in equity market leadership. With no near-term earnings on the calendar for the watchlist, next week’s trading will largely reflect how investors digest this latest factor rotation and position for the next leg of the cycle. The key will be to distinguish between transient short-covering and more durable re-rating, while staying anchored to the fundamental narratives that continue to drive long-term value creation across the AI and digital economy stack.[1]

High-beta growth outperformed as names like IONQ, HIMS, AFRM, and CRDO posted outsized weekly gains north of 30–60%, aided by short-covering and renewed enthusiasm around AI infrastructure and software leverage. Sector rotation favored software infrastructure, application software, cybersecurity, and semiconductors, while energy, fertilizers, and some cyclicals sold off as investors leaned back into duration and growth. Looking ahead, the tape will be driven more by macro catalysts such as the next FOMC decision, inflation prints, and labor data than near-term earnings, with positioning now more extended in long-duration tech and AI beneficiaries after a powerful multi-week run.
